strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing accuracy guarantees for influence function (IF) and Newton step (NS) data attribution rely on unrealistic global strong convexity (Assumption 1.6), and the authors clearly document why this fails even for unregularized logistic regression (Hessian decay with ||θ||) and how the resulting 1/λ³ dependence renders prior bounds vacuous in practice.

The main theoretical contribution (Theorem 1.11) is a clean, genuinely local condition—strong convexity and directional Lipschitzness only in a neighborhood of the first Newton step—and the proof (Section 3) is short, self-contained, and uses self-concordance-style arguments; this is a real relaxation of Theorem 1.3-style guarantees.

The concrete instantiation (Theorem 1.2 / Theorems B.2–B.4) provides almost-matching upper and lower bounds (up to polylog factors) on NS error and the IF–NS gap in Gaussian logistic regression, both for average-case and adversarial drop-sets, which to the authors' credit appears to be the first quantitative explanation of the empirical NS > IF phenomenon noted in [KATL19].

The analysis of RIF and the proposed DRIF correction (Theorems 1.12–1.13, Appendix F) is a nice bonus: it both explains a prior empirical observation and yields a simple, additive-structure-preserving method, validated in Figure 1 on synthetic and IMDB/BERT data.

The limitations section is honest and specific (purely theoretical, large-n regime n ≫ d², k², existence-only for non-convex losses, error norms rather than directions), and the appendices contain substantial detail supporting reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The regime restriction n ≫ k² + d² (equivalently k, d ≪ √n) is severe and limits practical reach; the paper only conjectures (Appendix C) that the scalings persist for k, d ≤ cn, and the most practically relevant modern setting (n comparable to d, deep-net attribution via TRAK-style reductions) is not covered. The headline claim of 'resolving open questions' is thus narrower than the abstract suggests.

The sharp quantitative results (Theorem 1.2) hold only for the deliberately simple Gaussian logistic regression toy model with ||θ*|| = Θ(1); the connection back to realistic data (covariate distributions with unbounded norms, adversarial structure, non-convex models) is left informal ('we believe our results provide insight into scaling laws… for a wide range of ERM-based estimators'), which is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Several proof steps are only sketched or rely on omitted/hand-waved arguments: the proof of Lemma H.13 is omitted entirely; the net-and-rearrangement argument in Lemma H.4 is compressed to the point of being hard to verify ('which rearranges to what we wanted to show'); and parts of the lower-bound chain (Lemmas D.2–D.6, Lemma E.4) combine many probability events whose joint failure probability accounting is not always made explicit.

The empirical validation is thin: a single figure with two settings, uniform random removals only, no quantitative comparison of observed scaling exponents against the predicted Θe(·) rates, and no experimental illustration of the adversarial drop-set regime where the theory is arguably most novel.

The general-purpose Theorem 1.11 is quantitatively coarse (the bound ‖θ̂loc − θ̂NS‖_Σ ≤ ChCop is only useful when the constants can be evaluated, which the authors themselves acknowledge is the motivation for the toy-model analysis), and Assumption 1.10 (ChCop < r) embeds a circularity concern that is discussed but only resolved within the Gaussian model.

There are presentation defects that undermine confidence: 'Proof Theorem 1.7' in Appendix A, an incomplete sentence in Section 1.3 ('Global Strong Convexity via Regularization is Inadequate One approach to justifying this argument…'), notation drifting between H, H_T, H_{θ̂T′} across appendices, and worst-case bounds stated as Θ(Θe(·)) in Theorem B.4 where only upper bounds are actually proven for RIF/DRIF in some regimes.
